title: Sri Lanka joins Orange Movement, opens access to  $ 500 m funding pool by 2030 | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 29 October 2026 05:45
-     - 56

Sri Lanka yesterday formally joined the global Orange Movement as the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) and the Impact Investment Exchange (IIX) signed an MoU to bring Orange Bonds into the local capital market. 

Orange Bonds channel capital to gender equality and climate resilience. The CSE also announced completion of the framework for the country’s first two Orange Bonds, with issuance targeted by December 2026. Alliance Finance Company PLC, named by CSE CEO Rajeeva Bandaranaike as the first issuer, plans to raise Rs. 1 billion through Orange Bonds, while the second company is still working out details.

The MoU was signed at the Orange Economy Summit 2026 in Colombo, convened by IIX with the Lanka Impact Investing Network (LIIN) and the CSE. The summit brought together senior Government representatives, capital market regulators, development partners, investors and financial institutions.

The MoU integrates the Orange Bond Principles into the CSE’s Green, Blue, Social, Sustainability and Sustainability-Linked (GSS+) Bond regulatory framework, which became effective last year and is based on principles of the International Capital Market Association. This allows future issuers to access the Orange Bond market through existing listing infrastructure, removing a structural barrier to market growth.

IIX also launched a research paper on financing Sri Lanka’s Orange Economy. The paper sets a target of accessing $ 500 million in Orange Capital mobilised by 2030 for South Asia, a pool now open to Sri Lanka. It also targets an increase in women-owned enterprises’ share of MSME lending from 28% to 35% by value.

Figures presented at the summit showed that women-owned enterprises accounted for 46% of MSME loans by number but only 28% by value, while their non-performing loans were lower at every reporting bank. IIX described them as an underpriced, underserved and high-quality customer base.

IIX plans to work with the CSE and issuers to bring the first Orange Bond issuers to market by December. One issuer has already announced its plans, with pricing a key consideration. IIX will also develop an investment readiness standard with local enterprises and issuers so that more Orange Bonds can be issued under the framework. It will also work with enterprises, investors and issuers to make impact measurement central to raising capital.

IIX positioned the Orange Movement as a business opportunity rather than corporate social responsibility, saying first movers would win customers, capital and reputation. It urged banks and financial institutions to identify their Orange portfolios and develop their first Orange products. It also called on development partners and investors to provide guarantees and catalytic capital to help reach the 2030 target.

The Orange Movement, launched by IIX and its partners in 2022, is the world’s largest coordinated initiative to mobilise private capital for gender equality and climate resilience. It aims to mobilise $ 15 billion by 2030 to empower 150 million women and underserved communities worldwide, with $ 500 million earmarked for South Asia. IIX Founder and CEO Prof. Durreen Shahnaz said that in four years the movement had reached six continents, mobilised over $ 2 billion and impacted 3.5 million lives.

Prof. Shahnaz said IIX had committed to reaching more than 1.2 million women and their families in Sri Lanka by 2030. She said IIX had invested close to $ 8 million in Sri Lanka so far, reaching over 8,000 lives, most of them women and their families.

Referring to the South Asia allocation, Prof. Shahnaz said: “If Sri Lanka’s markets and institutions are ready, a significant share of the capital can be invested right here.” “I urge you not to treat this summit as a ceremony. Treat it as a starting line. Make a pledge to bring the Orange Movement into your institution, your portfolio and your market,” she said.

Prof. Shahnaz noted that only 32% of Sri Lankan women were in the labour force, describing the gap as ‘growth left on the table’. A quarter of working women were employed in agriculture, and smallholder farmers, fishing families and women running businesses from home were the first to be hit when Cyclone Ditwah struck last year, she said.

“Sri Lanka has set itself the goal of growth of about 7% to become a $ 120 billion economy by 2030. Public finances alone cannot carry that growth target. Bring in women, minority communities, persons with disabilities, and the 7% growth target stops being a stretch,” Prof. Shahnaz said.

LIIN Chairman Chandula Abeywickrema said high borrowing costs remained a major obstacle for small businesses, with micro-entrepreneurs paying interest rates of 14% to 20%, and sometimes as high as 30%. “How can any entrepreneur pay that kind of interest?” he asked.

Drawing on four decades in banking and finance in Sri Lanka and Asia, Abeywickrema said a country’s future development would be measured not by how many people worked as employees in the public and private sectors, but by how many entrepreneurs it had. He said LIIN had pioneered access to private equity for entrepreneurs, the first such initiative in Sri Lanka.

Abeywickrema said capital should not be restrictive and must come in different forms to suit different sectors and people, while being available, accessible and affordable. Entrepreneurs also needed hand-holding, not just loans or grants, he said.

Bandaranaike said the CSE was in talks with other prospective issuers and was sure Alliance Finance Company PLC’s move would encourage many of them to follow a similar path.

He said women were one of the most significant sources of untapped economic potential in Sri Lanka. Many still faced obstacles in accessing finance, expanding their businesses and entering new markets, leaving commercially viable enterprises undercapitalised, he said.

He said Orange Bonds were not confined to a single industry. They applied a gender lens across the economy and treated gender inclusion as an investable economic opportunity, opening the market to financial institutions, corporates and other entities, he said.

However, he cautioned that good intentions alone did not make a successful financial instrument. An Orange Bond must be backed by sound financial fundamentals, appropriate governance, transparent use of proceeds and reliable impact measurement, he said. “The social objective cannot be a substitute for financial discipline. Rather, the two must reinforce each other.”

Bandaranaike said Sri Lanka’s capital market had recorded over 12 GSS+ Bond issuances, mobilising more than Rs. 90 billion, and that GSS+ Bonds accounted for 40% of listed debt raised last year.

“The true value of a capital market should not be measured only by the capital it mobilises, but also by the economic opportunities that capital helps create,” he said. “When we invest in women’s potential, we are not merely investing in women, we are investing in the future of our economy.”

title: AFC to raise Rs. 1 b via Sri Lanka’s first Orange Bond | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 29 October 2026 05:41
-     - 46

AFC Managing Director Romani De Silva - Pic by Shehan Gunasekara

Alliance Finance Company PLC (AFC) yesterday said its Board of Directors had approved raising up to Rs. 1 billion through an Orange Bond issue, set to be the first Orange Bond listed in Sri Lanka.

The Board resolved on 27 October, 2026 to issue up to 10 million listed, rated, unsecured, redeemable three-year Bonds at a par value of Rs. 100 each, the company said. The pricing of the Bonds will be announced later.

Proceeds are intended for eligible social project categories, including MSME Value Chain Financing, MSME Climate Financing and Micro Finance directed towards women-led enterprises and female beneficiaries. The issue is subject to regulatory clearances. MSMEs are micro, small and medium enterprises.

Alliance Finance Managing Director Romani de Silva, speaking on a panel at the Orange Economy Summit 2026 in Colombo, convened by IIX with the Lanka Impact Investing Network (LIIN) and the CSE, said women accounted for around 35% of the company’s lending portfolio, a level it was not happy with. “Our intention is to get it to 50% as soon as possible. Hence the interest in issuing an Orange Bond,” he said.

De Silva said Alliance Finance mobilises about 82% of its funding from the Western Province, the country’s richest, and disburses about 72% to marginalised provinces. The North and East account for 14% of its portfolio.

The company lends mainly at market rates, while trying to keep the differential as low as possible. De Silva said funding from overseas had allowed it to unlock European Commission funds under the (European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus) initiative. These funds cover hedging costs and currency risk, cutting lending rates by 200 to 300 basis points, or 2 to 3 percentage points.

Founded in 1956, Alliance Finance became Sri Lanka’s first triple bottom line financial institution in 2012, measuring its performance on social and environmental outcomes alongside profit, De Silva said. He said the company had issued Sri Lanka’s first social Bond about a year ago. Orange Bonds were stronger, he said, in defining measurable outcomes for gender equality under the UN’s Sustainable Development Goal 5.

De Silva said the company put impact first and profit after. “When you create immense value, it usually transforms into financial value as well. But you can’t do it the other way around,” he said. He added that Alliance Finance had recorded the highest stock price growth in its sector over the last five years, with a return of 521%. This was not by design, but an outcome of placing communities first,” he said.

title: President, tourism industry discuss sweeping reforms | Daily FT

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and tourism industry representatives yesterday discussed a raft of regulatory reforms and expansion plans aimed at earning $ 10 billion in tourism revenue and attracting five million tourists by 2030, the President’s Office said.

Among the proposed reforms, all tourist hotels and accommodation providers would be brought under the relevant legal framework by requiring them to register with the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA), with the aim of formalising the industry.

Special attention was also given to introducing laws and regulations to govern businesses run by foreign nationals in Sri Lanka in violation of prescribed legal procedures.

Participants discussed using national parks to support tourism growth, alongside new laws and regulations to protect forest resources.

On expansion, the meeting at the Presidential Secretariat noted that 10 new international airlines had begun flights to Sri Lanka this year, and discussed measures required to increase the number to 50.

Particular attention was given to improving domestic air travel, especially to Trincomalee, Batticaloa, Sigiriya and Jaffna. Progress on global campaigns currently underway to promote Sri Lanka’s tourism industry was also reviewed.

Labour Minister and Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando, Secretary to the President Dr. Nandika Sanath Kumanayake, Sri Lanka Hotels Association President Ashoka Hettigoda and Sri Lanka Inbound Tour Operators Association President Bobby Jordan Hansen were among those present. Members of the task force set up to promote tourism also attended.

The 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit 2026 yesterday announced that Pinnacle Distribution Lanka Ltd, together with VMware by Broadcom, has joined as a Gold Partner. 

This strategic collaboration brings one of the world’s most trusted names in enterprise infrastructure security to Sri Lanka’s premier cybersecurity event, reinforcing the summit’s mission to equip organisations with the knowledge and tools to confront AI-powered cyber threats.

Sri Lanka’s premier cybersecurity event, the 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit, organised by CICRA and the Daily FT will be held on 18 and 19 November at the Cinnamon Grand, Colombo.

Pinnacle Distribution Lanka is a leading value-added IT distribution and consulting company serving Sri Lanka and the Maldives, with over a decade of expertise in delivering enterprise-focused solutions. As a Broadcom Expert Advantage Partner and the VMware Partner of the Year 2025 (Rising Star – APAC), Pinnacle specialises in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), VMware vSAN, VMware Kubernetes Service (VKS), and the Tanzu Platform.

 The company provides end-to-end consulting services from infrastructure assessments and solution architecture design to project implementation and continuous optimisation helping enterprises to modernise their IT infrastructure with resilience and operational efficiency.

CICRA Holdings Group Executive Director/CEO Boshan Dayaratne said:  “We are delighted to welcome VMware and thank Pinnacle for coming on board as a Gold Partner for the 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit.” 

“The threat landscape is no longer static. AI is changing the volume, velocity, and variety of attacks, and traditional perimeter-based security is insufficient. What organisations need today is layered, infrastructure-native defence the kind of zero-trust, hypervisor-level protection that VMware and Pinnacle bring to the table. This partnership ensures our summit attendees gain direct access to the technologies and expertise that will define the next generation of cyber resilience,” he added. 

Pinnacle Distribution Lanka Ltd., Managing Director Saman D. Perera said: “Pinnacle is proud to partner with CICRA and VMware as a Gold Partner for the 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit. VMware’s security innovations, particularly vDefend, Avi Load Balancer, and the newly launched HyperArmor, represent a fundamental shift toward proactive, infrastructure embedded defense. As Sri Lankan enterprises accelerate their digital transformation and adopt AI-driven operations, the need for resilient, secure foundations has never been greater. We look forward to engaging with summit participants and demonstrating how Pinnacle and VMware can help them build that foundation.”

At the summit, Pinnacle and VMware will introduce attendees to VMware’s comprehensive security solutions designed for the AI era. VMware’s security portfolio delivers comprehensive endpoint and network visibility, detection and response, and zero-trust implementation to defend against ransomware and pinpoint threats with strong lateral security. 

Key products on display will include: VMware vDefend: Delivers strong lateral security with micro-segmentation and advanced threat detection and prevention for VMware Cloud Foundation workloads; VMware AVI Load Balancer: Provides web application and API protection (WAAP) for securing web and API traffic; VMware HyperArmour: A newly introduced solution offering proactive, zero-day protection for the VMware ESX hypervisor component of VMware Cloud Foundation, with no downtime, software upgrades, or in-guest agents required. As AI-accelerated threats grow in scale and sophistication, HyperArmour closes exposure windows by allowing only what is “known good” to run on the host, delivering virtual patching and positive security guardrails at the infrastructure layer.

The 12th Annual Cyber Security Summit  is entirely focused on the latest technological advance Artificial Intelligence and is dedicated to answering the critical question: “Is your organisation ready for AI-based cyber attacks?” Day one, 18 November, features the invitation-only CEO Forum on “Why Cyber Security Should Be a Boardroom Discussion,” addressing board-level liability under the Companies Act and PDPA and the urgent need for robust AI governance frameworks. 19 November is the full-day conference, bringing global expert speakers, a world-renowned Capture the Flag challenge, and invaluable insights and solutions for attendees and that same evening, the famous “Night Hack” event delivers a thrilling night of AI hacking and defending, giving participants a live, hands-on look at the real-world implications of AI-powered threats. The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) yesterday said it has added Max App Media Ltd. and two affiliated companies to its list of prohibited pyramid schemes, taking the total to 27.

The CBSL said that investigations had determined that Max App Media Ltd., and its affiliates, Max LK Ltd., and Max Media Lanka Ltd., had engaged in, conducted and promoted a prohibited pyramid scheme. Pyramid schemes pay returns to members largely from money brought in by new recruits rather than from genuine business activity.

The determination was made under Section 83(C) of the Banking Act, No. 30 of 1988, as amended.

The list, published through the CBSL’s Financial Consumer Relations Department, includes companies and applications previously identified as prohibited. They include Tiens Lanka Health Care Ltd., Best Life International Ltd., Sport Chain, OnmaxDT, MTFE, Fastwin Ltd., Qnet/Questnet, Ledger Block, Beecoin App and TM App.

title: Flexiprint: A Top Ten triumph, a silver standard of excellence and a legacy that inspires | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 29 October 2026 05:09
-     - 21

Sathis Abeywickrama receiving the top 10 award

Sathis Abeywickrama receiving Silver award

Flexiprint Team

Sri Lankan manufacturing excellence recognised at the CNCI Achiever Awards 2026

In a proud celebration of industrial excellence, innovation and national achievement, Flexiprint Ltd., secured two prestigious accolades at the CNCI Achiever Awards 2026, held at Cinnamon Life, Colombo, on the evening of 15 October 2026. The company received the Silver Award in the National Level Manufacturing Sector – Extra Large Category and was recognised with a Top Ten Award, reinforcing its position as a leading force in Sri Lanka’s printing and packaging industry.

These accolades represent far more than trophies. They recognise a company built on entrepreneurial vision, technological advancement, manufacturing expertise and customer trust. This achievement belongs to the entire Flexiprint family its sales and marketing teams, management, skilled workforce, operational personnel and stakeholders. Above all, it reflects the confidence of customers in Sri Lanka and international markets, whose continued partnership has been instrumental in the company’s growth.

From a local vision to international recognition

Founded by Managing Director Sathis Abeywickrama, Flexiprint was built on an understanding of the specialised printing requirements of Sri Lanka’s tea industry. Recognising the need for reliable, high-quality tea packaging components, the company invested in developing local manufacturing capabilities that could meet demanding customer specifications and international expectations.

What began as a focused response to an industry requirement has grown into a sophisticated manufacturing operation serving customers across multiple markets. Flexiprint’s journey reflects its founder’s commercial foresight, determination and commitment to building a business that competes on quality, reliability and innovation.

Rather than simply following industry developments, the company has continually sought to anticipate customer needs, embrace modern technology and expand its manufacturing capabilities. Its latest CNCI recognition stands as an encouraging endorsement of that commitment.

A trusted partner to Sri Lanka’s tea industry

Ceylon Tea is one of Sri Lanka’s most recognised export products, carrying the country’s reputation to consumers around the world. Behind every successful tea brand is a supply chain that depends on quality, consistency, presentation and timely delivery.

Flexiprint plays an important role in supporting this industry by manufacturing and supplying specialised products, including tea bag tags, tea envelopes, pyramid tea bag mesh and tags, alongside other customised printing solutions.

Although these components may be small in size, their contribution to product presentation, brand identity and packaging functionality is significant. Tea tags communicate a brand’s identity, envelopes contribute to product protection and presentation, while pyramid tea bag mesh supports the premium tea experience increasingly sought by consumers worldwide.

Flexiprint understands the precision and reliability required in this specialised field. Its manufacturing capabilities help tea producers and exporters access essential packaging components from a dependable partner that understands their requirements and the demands of international markets.

By strengthening local supply capabilities, Flexiprint contributes to the competitiveness of Sri Lankan tea businesses while supporting customers overseas who depend on consistent, high-quality production.

Beyond tea: Supporting FMCG and other brands worldwide

Flexiprint’s expertise extends well beyond the tea industry. Through its label-printing capabilities, the company serves the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector and other industries with self-adhesive labels, product labels, printed stickers and customised labelling solutions.

From everyday consumer products to specialised packaging applications, labels are a vital part of brand communication. They must combine visual appeal with printing precision, durability and consistent quality.

Flexiprint brings together technical expertise and modern production capabilities to help businesses translate their brand identities into high-quality printed materials. Its diversification reflects a forward-looking strategy: building on established strengths while responding to evolving customer requirements across industries and international markets.

For customers, the value extends beyond the finished product. It lies in having a manufacturing partner capable of understanding specifications, maintaining consistency, managing demanding production schedules and delivering dependable service.

Technology, infrastructure and internationally aligned standards

At the heart of Flexiprint’s competitiveness is its commitment to modern manufacturing. Investments in advanced printing machinery, specialised production systems, colour-management technology and quality-control processes enable the company to meet demanding production requirements while pursuing greater efficiency and consistency.

In an increasingly competitive global marketplace, manufacturers cannot afford to stand still. Customers expect higher quality, greater flexibility, shorter lead times and responsible production practices. Flexiprint recognises that sustained success requires continuous investment in machinery, infrastructure, technical knowledge and process improvement.

Technology alone, however, does not guarantee excellence. It is the combination of modern equipment, effective production, experienced personnel and rigorous quality monitoring that turns investment into performance.

The company’s emphasis on internationally recognised standards and compliance further supports its ambitions. Its published credentials include FSSC 22000 Version 6 and ISO 14001:2015, alongside PEFC related credentials and SEDEX membership. These frameworks reflect important commitments relating to food safety, environmental management, responsible sourcing and ethical business practices.

For companies serving international markets, such standards are increasingly important. Global competitiveness requires more than manufacturing capacity; it demands consistency, accountability and the ability to meet the expectations of customers and markets worldwide.

The people behind the performance

Behind every successful manufacturing operation are people whose knowledge, skill and commitment transform technology into results.

At Flexiprint, its well-trained workforce, capable machine operators, technical specialists and operational teams are central to the company’s achievements. Their contribution ensures that complex production processes are managed efficiently and that quality remains a priority at every stage.

Printing excellence requires far more than operating machinery. It demands technical understanding, attention to detail, colour judgement, troubleshooting skills and the discipline to maintain exacting standards under demanding production schedules. Equally important are the operational teams responsible for coordinating materials, production planning, quality checks, maintenance and dispatch.

Sales and marketing teams connect these capabilities with customer expectations, while management provides strategic direction and the resources required for continued progress.

Every successful order is therefore a collective accomplishment. The CNCI awards belong to everyone who contributes to Flexiprint’s performance from those who build customer relationships to those who operate machines and ensure that finished products meet required standards.

The company’s workforce deserves to share fully in this recognition.

Customer confidence: The foundation of success

In export oriented industries, a supplier’s reliability can directly influence production schedules, shipment commitments and brand reputation. Quality, service and delivery are not optional extras; they are essential to maintaining business relationships.

Flexiprint’s relationships with tea manufacturers, exporters and customers across other industries reflect the importance of dependable service and technical competence. Its international reach demonstrates the opportunities available to Sri Lankan manufacturers that combine quality, capacity, responsiveness and value.

These relationships are the result of coordinated effort across the organisation. The sales and marketing teams deserve particular recognition for developing partnerships, understanding changing market requirements and translating customer expectations into manufacturing opportunities. Production and operational personnel, in turn, work to fulfil those commitments.

The contribution of customers must never be understated. Their trust, loyalty and continued business have helped create opportunities for investment, employment, innovation and growth. Flexiprint’s achievement is, in every sense, a shared success with its customers in Sri Lanka and around the world.

A founder’s vision and a legacy carried forward

Flexiprint’s journey is inseparable from the vision of its founder and Managing Director, Sathis Abeywickrama. His entrepreneurial foresight helped identify an opportunity in a strategically important export industry and turn it into a specialised manufacturing business with ambitions beyond the domestic market.

His leadership has been instrumental in establishing a culture centred on customer service, technical expertise, investment and continuous improvement. His philosophy recognises that lasting business success depends on more than commercial performance: it requires committed people, dependable partnerships and the willingness to keep moving forward.

Mr. Abeywickrama has previously emphasised the importance of careful planning, hard work and the dedication of the team, together with the trust customers have placed in Flexiprint over the years. That collective approach remains central to the company’s continuing progress.

Equally significant is the continuation of this legacy through his son, Isuru Abeywickrama. Carrying forward the foundations established by his father, he represents an important part of Flexiprint’s next chapter.

A legacy is not simply about preserving past achievements. It is about respecting the principles that created success while adapting to a changing business environment. For Flexiprint, that means embracing new technologies, developing talent, strengthening customer partnerships and exploring opportunities in evolving printing and packaging markets.

The company’s future will be shaped by its ability to combine the strength of its established reputation with the fresh thinking required for continued growth.

A proud milestone and a platform for greater success

The CNCI Achiever Awards 2026 mark an important milestone for Flexiprint and recognise the collective effort behind its progress. They honour the founder’s vision, the leadership carrying that vision forward, the commitment of management, the contribution of sales and marketing teams, the expertise of machine operators and operational personnel, and the support of its wider stakeholder network.

Most importantly, they celebrate the customers whose confidence has helped shape the company’s journey.

For Sri Lanka, Flexiprint’s achievement is also a reminder of the value of investing in specialised local manufacturing, skilled employment, modern infrastructure and export-oriented capabilities.

Yet the real measure of these awards will be what follows: the quality of products manufactured, the promises fulfilled, the people developed, the relationships strengthened and the standards upheld.

Two prestigious recognitions. One united team. A legacy built on vision. A future driven by innovation and customer confidence.

Flexiprint has every reason to celebrate this achievement with pride. It has demonstrated the strength of Sri Lankan manufacturing and reaffirmed its ambition to serve customers at home and across the globe.

Flexiprint, proudly Sri Lankan, globally connected, and relentlessly committed to excellence.

Held under the theme ‘Building Capacity, Creating Opportunities and Scaling Sri Lanka’s Digital Future,’ the flagship event is a landmark step toward positioning Sri Lanka as an emerging FinTech and digital economy hub within Asia. 

The festival aims to gather leaders from FinTech, banking, NBFI, technology and investment sectors with policymakers, regulators, international networks and regional partners, alongside entrepreneurs, SMEs and tourism-sector stakeholders.

Sri Lanka already has significant digital financial services infrastructure in place, including national payment rails and real-time account-to-account transfers. The festival will bring these capabilities into the spotlight, providing a national platform to showcase, connect, and advance the ecosystem, attracting international collaboration and investment, and open doors for broader market access.

Over two days, the festival will combine high-level networking with in-depth industry discussion. Proceedings open on 2 November with the exclusive invitation-only CEOs Night, gathering senior stakeholders including Banking/NBFI and FinTech CEOs, FinTech Forum board and advisory council, distinguished speakers, high-level Central Bank and government officials and sponsors.

The visit brought together high-profile international media engagement, discussions with Indian industry representatives, an exploration of innovation partnerships with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi, and outreach to the diplomatic community. The Deputy Minister also invited Indian businesses to participate in Sri Lanka Expo 2027, the country’s flagship international trade exhibition.

The highlight of the visit was the Deputy Minister’s participation in the NDTV World Summit 2026 on 22 October, where he joined a fireside conversation titled “Sri Lanka’s Economic Reset: Recovery, Resilience and the Road Ahead.” Held under the theme “A World Between Orders,” the Summit brought together political leaders, policymakers, diplomats, business leaders and other prominent international voices.

During the discussion, the Deputy Minister expressed Sri Lanka’s deep appreciation to the Government and people of India for their support during the economic crisis of 2022. Reflecting on the lessons of the crisis, he outlined the progress made in restoring financial stability, restructuring debt and implementing structural reforms. He emphasised that, while Sri Lanka had emerged from the crisis and achieved greater stability, the next challenge was to translate these gains into sustained economic growth.

The Deputy Minister also highlighted the importance of greater integration with global markets. Drawing on India’s experience of gradually opening its economy and strengthening its international economic connections, he pointed to Sri Lanka’s ongoing trade reforms, including the removal of para-tariffs, as part of efforts to improve competitiveness and facilitate further free-trade agreements.

Sri Lanka’s ambition, he explained, extended beyond economic recovery. The country was seeking to position itself as a regional hub for trade, industry, technology, research and development, logistics, value addition and skilled talent. He invited international investors to participate in this transformation, delivering a clear message: “Don’t just support Sri Lanka’s recovery, be part of its growth.”

The Deputy Minister identified manufacturing, agricultural value addition, logistics, renewable energy, marine industries and technology as sectors offering significant potential for collaboration between Sri Lanka and India. He also outlined plans to establish new industrial zones through the Ministry of Industry and Entrepreneurship Development and through the Board of Investment of Sri Lanka to expand industrial capacity and create opportunities for both domestic and international investors.

Emphasising the importance of a more conducive business environment, he highlighted efforts to simplify investment procedures, digitise public services and strengthen regulatory clarity.

Engagement with Indian business leaders representing the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), the Chamber for Industrial Trade and Economic Cooperation (CITEC), the National Association of Software and Service Companies (NASSCOM) and the Federation for Global Economic and Cultural Relations (FGECR) formed another important dimension of the visit. The meeting on 23 October provided an opportunity to explore how the longstanding relationship between Sri Lanka and India could be translated into stronger industrial, investment and commercial partnerships. Discussions focused on opportunities for Indian businesses to invest in Sri Lanka, collaborate with Sri Lankan enterprises, introduce technology and expertise, and develop stronger links with regional and international markets. Particular attention was given to sectors where the complementary strengths of the two economies could create mutual benefits, including manufacturing, information technology, renewable energy, logistics and value-added production.

The Deputy Minister also visited the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi on 23 October to explore opportunities for collaboration between India’s innovation ecosystem and Sri Lanka’s emerging startup sector. Discussions focused on India’s experience in developing startup incubation programmes, the institutional and legal frameworks supporting early-stage enterprises, and partnerships connecting universities, researchers, entrepreneurs, investors and the private sector; and exploring potential institutional partnerships, knowledge sharing and opportunities to connect Sri Lankan entrepreneurs with India’s innovation networks. The Deputy Minister also interacted with startups developing innovative solutions with the potential for global impact.

The Deputy Minister’s engagements with leading Indian media organisations, including NDTV, WION and Times Now, provided further opportunities to communicate Sri Lanka’s economic priorities and its interest in deepening economic cooperation with India. These engagements reinforced Sri Lanka’s message that the country is seeking not only to consolidate its recovery but also to attract investment, expand industrial capacity and build mutually beneficial partnerships with Indian businesses.

The Deputy Minister also met with several Ambassadors of countries with diplomatic missions resident in New Delhi that are accredited to Sri Lanka and explained Sri Lanka’s economic priorities, industrial development agenda and investment prospects, while encouraging stronger commercial engagement and support for Sri Lanka’s development objectives.

title: UNP, SJB: Longest defeat, shortest road to resurgence | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 29 October 2026 04:04
-     - 25

Should dock UNP as junior partner with SJB, under Sajith’s leadership

Sajith is the SJB ex-UNP personality with the broadest base, not limited to the urban areas

Neither SJB nor UNP has another figure with such popular rapport

The serial defeat of the SJB is the ‘genetically transmitted’ continuation of the decades-long crisis of the UNP, its parent party from which it has chosen not to cut the ideological, doctrinal-programmatic and narrative umbilical cord. If AKD and the JVP-NPP are to be defeated, a repetition of 2024 (and 2019)—yet another defeat and failure—are simply unaffordable; cannot be risked

If the AKD-JVP-NPP Government is to be defeated, it must be grasped that its victory was caused by the main Opposition party ‘snatching defeat from the jaws of victory’ from its competitor who had merely 3% of the vote and 3 seats.

This is the exact opposite of Ranasinghe Premadasa who ‘snatched victory from the jaws of defeat’ in 1988, beating the formidable Sirimavo Bandaranaike and prevailing over a lethal JVP boycott.

The serial defeat of the SJB is the ‘genetically transmitted’ continuation of the decades-long crisis of the UNP, its parent party from which it has chosen not to cut the ideological, doctrinal-programmatic and narrative umbilical cord.

If AKD and the JVP-NPP are to be defeated, a repetition of 2024 (and 2019)—yet another defeat and failure—are simply unaffordable; cannot be risked.

UNP’s Achilles Heel

The UNP was flawed from the outset. It was perceived as:

The party of the privileged traditional classes—which is why the left did so well at the 1947 General Election and came within striking distance of forming a Government, self-sabotaging by its own sectarian refusal to form a coalition with independents such as SWRD Bandaranaike.

Pro-Western and anti-national, unpatriotic.

Minoritarian, out of touch with the sentiments of the majority community.

These three strategic weaknesses caused the UNP Government within the first decade of Independence to:

Lose SWRD Bandaranaike (1951)

Have PM Dudley Senanayake ejected by the Hartal (1953)

Be swept out by the SWRD-led ‘Silent Revolution’ (1956).

These structural weaknesses of the post-Independence UNP were patched up sufficiently by the seven-party Senanayake coalition of 1965 to enable victory, but the superficiality of the change—there was no internal transformation of the UNP itself—caused the 1965 coalition Government to develop internal fissures on ethnic reforms (as did Yahapalanaya 2015-2019), and be defeated by a centre-left United Front that obtained the first ever two-thirds majority in Parliament in 1970.

Longest defeat

(A) Why was the Presidential election of 1988 the very last time that the voters elected the UNP to lead the country?

(B) Why did this long failure continue in the UNP-derivative successor party and ‘offspring’ the SJB, which still calls the UNP its ‘parent’?

(C) Why hasn’t a UNP or UNP-derivative/para-UNP leader been elected to lead the country by popular vote for 38 years and counting—over three-and-a-half decades?

(D) Why did it take this country less time to defeat Prabhakaran and the LTTE, than it is taking for the UNP and its derivative the SJB to be elected to lead the country?

(E) Why did the JVP recover from devastating military defeat (1989) and be popularly elected to the presidency in a shorter duration (2024) than the UNP and its SJB successor?

That’s because the UNP:

(i) Turned its back on the scientific formula that pulled it out of a deep rut in the 1970-1977 period, saved it from physical extinction in 1988-1989, and kept it on top until 1993 when the LTTE assassinated the formula’s author.

(ii) Never returned to the socioeconomic policy paradigm that kept the UNP winning elections during that period of exception.

Inexplicably, the successor SJB didn’t act rationally and return to the formula that saved the UNP twice, nor to the policy paradigm that ensured economic success and electoral popularity.

After the UNP Government sabotaged President Premadasa’s funeral in May 1993, turning away the huge crowds coming into Colombo by declaring a curfew on specious grounds, and then proceeded to dump Premadasa’s policy paradigm, discourse and team, it never won a Presidential election.

It took almost 15 years between the first (2001) and second (2015) time Ranil’s UNP held the Prime Ministership.

Even after Ranil Wickremesinghe was selected by Parliament as President and ran at the Presidential election in 2024 having ‘stabilised’ the economy, and enjoying the backing of SLFP-SLPP defectors (‘Gas Cylinder’), he won only 20% of the vote, coming third. Sajith beat him by 12%.

The UNP was subjected to four-prolonged exposures to politico-ideological ‘Kryptonite’.

1. After President Premadasa’s assassination, the UNP had the choice of a Ranil Wickremesinghe-Karu Jayasuriya-Sirisena Cooray troika, proceeding along a neo-Premadasaist path, consolidating the electoral base built by the various programs of President Premadasa. Instead, the anti-Premadasa breakaway faction, the DUNF which arose out of the impeachment conspiracy, was unconditionally re-inducted into the post-Premadasa UNP; the Premadasa image and programs were jettisoned.

2. Ranil affiliated the UNP with the International Democratic Union (IDU) of the global conservative, right-wing and centre-right. This ended the Premadasa populist-social democratic orientation in and of the UNP, losing the party’s appeal to and votes of the underprivileged, rendering it reliant on the minorities. Since the SJB inherited and embraced the IDU and International Republican Institute nexus, the ability to learn from and play the role of the US Democrats and UK Labour has been blocked.

3. Ranil Wickremesinghe signed the Liam Fox agreement committing the UNP to a negotiated solution with the Tigers. The claim that Ranil’s Ceasefire Agreement with Prabhakaran split the LTTE and helped win the war, paled into pathetic insignificance when compared to the military downside of Ranil’s appeasement and Mahinda Rajapaksa’s victorious, historically indelible war-time leadership.

4. The UNP (containing today’s SJB members) compounded its wartime blunders during the postwar Yahapalanaya years 2015-2019 by co-sponsoring with the West, a resolution at the UNHRC in Geneva (2015) supporting a hybrid court with international participation to judge allegations of war crimes and crimes against humanity. This confirmed the long-held public perception—with President Premadasa as outstanding exception—that the UNP was supinely pro-Western, unpatriotic.

Cumulatively these deviations resulted in the longest stretch of continuous electoral defeat of a politico-ideological ‘brand’ and project at Presidential elections, extending from 1994 to date.

Principles and formula for victory

In the crucible of the harsh authoritarianism and mass austerity of the SLFP-LSSP-CPSL Government wielding the island’s first-ever 2/3rds majority, the UNP in Opposition transformed itself from a party with a paltry 17 MPs in Parliament to one that won a 5/6ths majority within a single term in 1977.

That transformation which generated the 1977 victory ushered in the Open Economy. But the choice not to adhere to that formula in the post-1977 period (despite warnings from the formula’s author), contributed to the Southern social uprising of the 1980s that threatened the UNP’s very survival.

In this hour of the UNP’s high-intensity existential crisis (1988), the party turned to the principal author of the formula which had transformed the UNP from the twice-defeated party of 1956 and 1970 into the winning party of 1977. The return to that formula (of 1973-1977), enabled the UNP win the 1988 Presidential Election, the 1989 Parliamentary Election, and defeat Wijeweera’s JVP by November 1989. It also enabled the ruling UNP to win the Local Government election of 1991 despite the impact of the impeachment motion of that year, which had been rolled-back.

What then are (a) the formula, the principles, for turning UNP-SJB defeat into success and (b) the doctrine for socioeconomic success in Government, which the UNP abandoned and the SJB never adopted?

Here’s the testimony of Lalith Athulathmudali, no fan of the formula’s author, writing on the UNP’s history as Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1980 in the Lanka Guardian retrospective Special issue on the 1970s:

“… It [the UNP] had to change its image in theory and in practice. It had to stand on the side of the underprivileged; it had to provide answers to their problems.

The one-rupee membership campaign not only changed the money sources of the party but it also helped to democratise its internal politics.

A new policy and program proposed by a committee headed by R. Premadasa was adopted.

Family power and privileged group power were dethroned and the fact that these very monstrosities were being strengthened in the other parties only served to consolidate the UNP.

In the popular mind the UNP often thought of as being concerned with the few, came to be considered as the party of the masses. The UNP had built itself a new political base”.

(Lanka Guardian, Vol. 2 No 17, 1980 p13-14).

This describes the structural transformation of the party and its character. It had a backstory.

Frustrated by the Dudley Senanayake-led UNP’s slow pace and continued conventionality in Opposition, R. Premadasa had stepped away and formed the Puravesi Peramuna (Citizens’ Front), the island’s first populist-democratic party, embarking on a frontal offensive against the powerful Govt, holding packed public meetings at Hyde Park and other venues (1972-1973).

When Jayewardene assumed party leadership (1973), he invited Premadasa to return and re-make the UNP itself along the lines of his Citizens’ Front. Thus, the Puravesi Peramuna became the prototype of the restructured UNP which won the 5/6th majority landslide in 1977.

The second part of the winning formula pertained to project and paradigm, defined by Premadasa:

“…That in brief, is what JSP [Janasaviya Program] is all about…I see it as the basis for a new Political, Social and Economic Democracy.”

This is from President Premadasa’s interview given to Neville Jayaweera, re-submitted to him for amendments and approval, published as ‘Sri Lanka Towards a Multi-ethnic Democracy: Report of a Fact-Finding Mission’, International Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO),1990, Appendix 3, p 139. (https://www.prio.org/publications/14177)

“A New Political, Social and Economic Democracy” is the political ‘sutra’ that should have guided the UNP after Premadasa just as during his leadership, and should surely have been the basis on which the SJB was founded. But it wasn’t.

Structural stagnation

SWRD Bandaranaike and his SLFP, the core of which—including DA Rajapaksa—broke from DS Senanayake’s UNP (1951), never looked back, lost its first election (1952) but spectacularly won the second in five years since its founding (1956). However, the SJB left the UNP but always looked back in policy terms, never evolved its own distinctive ideology and identity. To this day it hasn’t or can’t state its distinctive identity and policies as demarcated from the UNP—even Ranil’s UNP.

Since the SJB preferred not to return to the Premadasa paradigm at its founding or in the years after, and regards itself as on a continuum with “our Government” by which it explicitly means the administrations of Wickremesinghe as PM (2001-4, 2015-2019), it has logically, inevitably shared the fate of the post-Premadasa UNP: defeat at Presidential elections.

Just as Ranil lost elections for six years, being elected PM only seven years after he became UNP leader, the SJB has lost parliamentary elections twice (and the crucial Colombo Municipal Council too) in the six years it has been in existence.

Unable to recognise that any serious political party is by definition primarily political, and to understand that James Carville’s watchword for Bill Clinton’s campaign, ‘It’s the economy, stupid!’, meant the attack on the Bush Sr. administration should focus on the economic hardships of the people, ‘Putting People First’ rather than statistics of economic performance, the SJB economic troika endorsed President Ranil Wickremesinghe’s stabilisation package which turned out to be one of the harshest austerity programs on the record globally. This compromising entanglement and role conflict cleared the space for the AKD-JVP-NPP victory in 2024.

In his last May day speech (1992) Premadasa said that had SWRD been alive he would have been on the UNP stage because under him (Premadasa) the UNP had changed to the extent that SWRD would have not felt compelled to leave as he did in 1951. Premadasa was always sensitive to the need to win over/win back the SLFP voter.

The SJB however, pitches to win with ‘generic’ UNP votes alone. The Dullas-GL group of 13 SLPP dissenters which had allied with the SJB, had been so marginalised and alienated by the ‘Blueprint’ neoliberals that they were unavailable to swing SLFP-SLPP votes for Sajith in 2024. AKD reaped those votes.

JR and Premadasa in Opposition were able to win massively in one term because they ‘put politics in command’ not liberal economic dogma, despite the extreme economic crisis. When Sirimavo pivoted rightwards, sacking Dr. NM Perera, the JR-Premadasa UNP escalated its attack on (foreign-investment seeking) Finance Minister Felix Dias Bandaranaike while moving No Confidence Motions with the LSSP against the Government. UNP stalwart Gamini Fonseka’s post-1977 film ‘Sagarayak Meda’ recreated the anti-Felix mood.

Sajith’s audience at Dehiattakandiya, Ampara district

The UNP has run out of road. Its only viable move is to do what it did in 1988: hand the leadership over to Premadasa, this time Sajith, and become the SJB’s junior partner. The SJB has to be restructured and reoriented, politically rectified and renovated along the ‘new social, political and economic democracy’ agenda, if it is to secure elections on schedule in 2029, lead a campaign for a victorious NO vote at a referendum, and not trip itself up yet again electorally

1965 scenario

Countering Wimal Weerawansa’s scenario based on the Buddhist monks’ march, that Sri Lanka is headed for ‘another 1956’ in 2029, the pro-SJB e-paper Mawrata counterposes an alternative scenario: ‘another 1965’, illustrated with photographs of Sirimavo Bandaranaike and Dudley Senanayake. In 1965, the UNP headed a coalition which beat the SLFP-LSSP alliance.

There are two  more conspicuous models of victory to inspire the SJB and UNP: Jayewardene 1977 and Premadasa 1988. Furthermore, the Dudley Senanayake UNP was the one that both JR Jayewardene and Ranasinghe Premadasa publicly dissented against, deviated from, and replaced, enabling their far more stunning victories.

Ironically, the Dudley Senanayake 1965 model which succeeded in winning the 1965 election, flies in the face of the SJB’s current practice. The hallmark of the UNP’s 1965 formula, crafted by strategist Esmond Wickremesinghe, brilliant former Trotskyist, was a broad coalition of ideologically diverse elements. By contrast, the hallmark of the SJB today is its unwillingness to form any ideologically pluralist equation.

Far from emulating the Dudley Senanayake 1965 model, the SJB seems unaware of the bedrock of the 7-party coalition: partnership with the father of the Marxist movement in Ceylon, Philip Gunawardena who was by no means a convert to UNP ideology when he was made Minister of Industries (in which role he excelled). SJB spokespersons and ideologues see any equation containing ideological disparity as counterproductive and dysfunctional. They should ponder why JR chose Ronnie de Mel of MEP-SLFP provenance and a brilliant left-leaning radical, as Finance Minister to pilot the Open Economy.

The hope generated by the in-gathering of all Opposition parties at the Opposition Leader’s office and chaired by him on 23 July, has been shattered. The ‘Marikkar Mode’ disintegrated at the last moment, the multi-party convergence that was building up under the SJB’s leadership for the Polduwa demonstration against 22A. The uncouth abruptness involved made even the UNP’s Navin Dissanayake pull out. It will probably take a minute before the full complement of Opposition leaders gathers under SJB chairmanship at No 30 again.

Conclusion

The SJB’s potential progress is blocked because the political culture of the post-Premadasa UNP, has come to inhere in its successor. Through transmission or osmosis, the UNP’s reflexes-habits-instincts, have caused sporadic, episodic action, lack of drive and direction, and absence of strategic initiative in the SJB.

The UNP has run out of road. Its only viable move is to do what it did in 1988: hand the leadership over to Premadasa, this time Sajith, and become the SJB’s junior partner.

The SJB has to be restructured and reoriented, politically rectified and renovated along the ‘new social, political and economic democracy’ agenda, if it is to secure elections on schedule in 2029, lead a campaign for a victorious NO vote at a referendum, and not trip itself up yet again electorally.

title: Sri Lanka wants to fight organised crime. Will it weaken justice in the process? | Daily FT
summary:
Thursday, 29 October 2026 00:28
-     - 15

Sri Lanka’s recurring political disappointment is not simply that governments fail to fulfil campaign promises, but that the demands of exercising and preserving authority can gradually displace the principles through which that authority was obtained. Reform often requires governments to relinquish powers they may find politically useful, making it considerably more difficult than promising change during an election. For the NPP, the organised crime Bill consequently represents more than a question of criminal justice policy; it tests whether the Government understands institutional transformation as a genuine redistribution of authority away from political control

The proposed organised crime law exposes a fundamental contradiction in Sri Lanka’s reform agenda: a government elected promising independent institutions and freedom from political interference is seeking extraordinary powers over detention, evidence and surveillance. The question is whether it will break the country’s cycle of concentrated authority or preserve it under another name

Sri Lanka has spent decades expanding the powers of the state without necessarily improving its capacity to deliver justice. From emergency regulations to counterterrorism legislation, successive governments have responded to threats against public security through exceptional legal authority, often without sufficiently addressing the institutional weaknesses that undermine investigations and prosecutions. The threats have frequently been genuine, but the assumption that greater coercive power necessarily produces more effective law enforcement deserves scrutiny. The Prevention of Organised Crimes Bill, gazetted on 6 October 2026, now exposes a deeper paradox: can a country repair its criminal justice institutions by relaxing the safeguards designed to hold them accountable?

Organised crime demands a serious response. Criminal networks exploit intimidation, illicit finance, corruption and weaknesses in prosecution, making stronger investigative coordination and international cooperation legitimate priorities. Yet the proposed legislation extends beyond these objectives, authorising prolonged executive detention, altering evidentiary protections and expanding investigative discretion. The concern is not simply that such powers could be abused, but that extraordinary authority may become a substitute for institutional competence, enabling greater control over suspects without necessarily improving the state’s ability to establish criminal responsibility. For the National People’s Power government, the legislation also presents a test of political consistency: whether its commitment to independent institutions extends to restricting the powers available to itself.

A promise of independence, an expansion of authority

The NPP’s 2024 legal reform program promised an independent, transparent and accountable judiciary, acknowledging that political interference and ineffective implementation had damaged public confidence in justice. The government subsequently advanced proposals for an independent public prosecutor and measures to strengthen judicial independence, suggesting an understanding that meaningful reform depends upon institutions capable of operating independently of political authority. Yet the organised crime Bill raises questions about how those commitments can be reconciled with the expansion of executive powers within the criminal justice system.

Clause 20 generally permits suspects to remain in police custody for up to 72 hours before being produced before a Magistrate, subject to statutory qualifications, while clause 21 empowers the Secretary to the Ministry responsible for the police to authorise renewable detention orders potentially extending to one year, with High Court supervision of subsequent extensions. More consequentially, clause 20 requires a Magistrate presented with an initial detention order to give effect to it, raising questions about the substantive independence of judicial scrutiny over restrictions on personal liberty. Judicial independence cannot be understood merely as the absence of politicians instructing judges how to decide cases; it must also encompass the courts’ authority to independently examine executive decisions affecting fundamental rights. Although these provisions do not establish political interference, their allocation of authority warrants scrutiny.

The timing sharpens the contradiction. The NPP promised to repeal the Prevention of Terrorism Act, whose history includes prolonged detention, allegations of torture and coerced confessions, yet the organised crime Bill contains comparable forms of exceptional detention and evidentiary departure. The two laws are not identical, but repealing a controversial statute while preserving similar mechanisms elsewhere raises questions about whether institutional reform changes the underlying distribution of power or merely rearranges the legal instruments through which it is exercised. A government’s commitment to institutional independence cannot be measured solely by the powers it abolishes, but also by those it declines to acquire.

When criminal procedure becomes an investigative shortcut

The PTA, introduced in 1979, offers a historical warning about exceptional legal powers becoming embedded in ordinary governance. The consequences are not merely historical: in June 2025, Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court ordered two police officers to personally pay Rs. 2 million in compensation to a man unlawfully arrested, detained and tortured during a 2019 investigation. Although the judgment concerned existing law rather than the proposed Bill, it demonstrates why custodial coercion cannot be dismissed as hypothetical, particularly when legislative changes would make police-recorded statements more consequential in criminal proceedings.

Clauses 46 and 47 display sections 25, 26 and 30 of the Evidence Ordinance and permit certain signed statements, including confessions made to sufficiently senior police officers, to become admissible. The Bill provides safeguards concerning legal advice and audiovisual recording, but these protections do not entirely resolve the unequal relationship between interrogator and detainee, particularly where prolonged custody is permitted. Clause 48 also allows certain Magistrate-recorded statements from unavailable witnesses to be admitted without cross-examination, while clause 23 restricts bail in specified circumstances, although it provides for release on bail where remand reaches one year without indictment. These qualifications matter, but their cumulative interaction with extended detention and exceptional evidentiary rules requires careful examination.

Clause 25 introduces an additional mechanism through which an individual already held on remand may be transferred back into police custody, potentially in isolation, for periods cumulatively extending to six months. Although the provision requires an Attorney General’s application, a High Court inquiry, judicial review every 14 days and notification to the Human Rights Commission, returning an individual from judicial remand to investigative custody raises concerns about custodial pressure and the practical ability to exercise legal rights. The issue is not whether further investigation can ever justify additional custody, but whether such prolonged restrictions on liberty remain necessary and proportionate when less intrusive alternatives may exist. Article 13 of the Constitution protects against arbitrary arrest, guarantees fair-trial rights and recognises the presumption of innocence, principles that must remain central to any assessment of the Bill. A capable criminal justice system should make evidence more reliable, not merely easier to admit.

Powers, protections and the accountability deficit

The institutional tension extends to clause 59, which provides protection against civil or criminal proceedings for lawful acts undertaken in good faith under the legislation, including purported acts performed pursuant to its provisions. Such protections are not inherently illegitimate, since officers performing lawful investigative duties should not face vexatious proceedings simply because their actions are controversial, and the clause does not expressly immunise torture or unlawful violence. Nevertheless, its wording raises questions about how effectively citizens can challenge claims of good faith and whether meaningful remedies remain available when officials exceed their lawful authority.

This concern becomes more consequential when considered alongside the Bill’s wider investigative powers. Clauses 44 and 45 establish mechanisms for obtaining communications information and accessing encrypted data, while clause 14 restricts publication concerning specified criminal proceedings. These measures may serve legitimate objectives, including protecting victims and investigating complex criminal networks, but privacy, freedom of expression and public scrutiny cannot become incidental considerations. The principle of proportionality requires that intrusive measures be demonstrably necessary and subject to independent oversight. Where exceptional detention, altered evidentiary protections and safeguards for officials operate within the same legislative framework, the question is whether accountability expands alongside authority or becomes increasingly difficult to enforce.

When accountability risks appearing as vengeance

The concentration of extraordinary criminal powers also creates the risk of politically selective enforcement, or at least the public perception of it, particularly where detention decisions originate within the executive and politically sensitive prosecutions are involved. This does not establish that the NPP intends political revenge, nor should legitimate investigations into former political figures automatically be characterised as vindictive. Accountability requires impartial investigations based on evidence, while vengeance begins when political identity becomes more important than criminal responsibility. The greater the discretion afforded to officials, the more important it becomes to establish institutional safeguards capable of demonstrating that prosecutions are independent of political interests.

Sri Lanka’s political history makes this distinction particularly important. Successive governments have promised to confront corruption, patronage and interference in state institutions, yet the temptation to preserve powers previously criticised has remained a recurring concern. The JVP, a principal constituent of the NPP, has a history that includes armed insurrections in 1971 and 1987–89, although the contemporary NPP is a broader democratic coalition and cannot be reduced to that past. Its transition into government nevertheless presents an opportunity to demonstrate that political change can mean institutional restraint rather than another transfer of concentrated authority. Nelson Mandela’s approach to South Africa’s transition offers a limited parallel in distinguishing accountability from retaliation, although reconciliation there remained imperfect. The relevant principle is that durable democratic change requires institutions capable of administering justice independently of those who exercise political power.

International obligations are not unlimited authority

The government’s justification deserves serious consideration. Organised criminal networks operate across borders, conceal illicit proceeds and intimidate witnesses, creating genuine difficulties for conventional law enforcement. However, identifying such difficulties does not establish the necessity of every extraordinary power proposed. The United Nations Convention against Transnational Organised Crime promotes criminalisation, confiscation of illicit assets, witness protection and international cooperation, but it does not require year-long executive detention or police-admissible confessions. Article 20 expressly recognises that special investigative techniques must operate within the basic principles of domestic legal systems.

International comparisons illustrate alternative institutional priorities. Italy’s anti-mafia framework combines specialised investigations, financial intelligence and judicial mechanisms targeting criminal assets, while Britain’s unexplained wealth order regime requires applications to the High Court before authorities may compel explanations concerning certain suspiciously acquired property. Neither framework is without controversy, but both demonstrate methods of confronting the economic and organisational foundations of criminal networks without treating prolonged detention as the principal measure of investigative effectiveness.

Sri Lanka should therefore establish which existing investigative powers have proved inadequate, what evidence demonstrates that prolonged executive detention improves prosecution outcomes and why narrower, judicially supervised alternatives would be insufficient. Stronger financial intelligence, forensic investigation, witness protection, independent custody monitoring and enforceable access to counsel would address institutional weaknesses more directly. The Centre for Policy Alternatives has warned that the Bill risks creating a parallel detention framework and undermining ordinary criminal-law protections, concerns that deserve substantive parliamentary consideration rather than dismissal as opposition to public security.

An opportunity to break the cycle

Sri Lanka’s recurring political disappointment is not simply that governments fail to fulfil campaign promises, but that the demands of exercising and preserving authority can gradually displace the principles through which that authority was obtained. Reform often requires governments to relinquish powers they may find politically useful, making it considerably more difficult than promising change during an election. For the NPP, the organised crime Bill consequently represents more than a question of criminal justice policy; it tests whether the government understands institutional transformation as a genuine redistribution of authority away from political control.

The administration still has an opportunity to address legal criticism, narrow unnecessarily broad powers and establish stronger safeguards without abandoning its responsibility to confront organised crime. Such revisions would not demonstrate weakness, but a recognition that effective enforcement depends on the independence and competence of institutions rather than the accumulation of executive discretion. Laws endure beyond individual governments, and powers introduced today may eventually be exercised by administrations with different priorities and standards of accountability. Constitutional safeguards exist precisely because the protection of liberty cannot depend on the goodwill of those temporarily entrusted with authority.

Sri Lanka needs institutions capable of confronting organised crime decisively, but their strength must be measured by reliable investigations, independent courts and credible convictions rather than the breadth of their authority to detain, interrogate or surveil. The danger is not merely that Sri Lanka may give weak criminal justice institutions too much power, but that doing so could diminish the pressure to make them stronger. The NPP’s opportunity to break with the past lies not in acquiring the extraordinary authority sought by previous governments, but in demonstrating that effective justice can be achieved without depending upon it.

(The author is an International Relations student at Monash University whose writing explores politics, governance, and international affairs)

title: Future of Sri Lanka’s transport: 3 priorities for national progress | Daily FT

Thursday, 29 October 2026 00:24

Railway modernisation offers Sri Lanka an opportunity to build on its existing infrastructure and ongoing development partnerships

By prioritising practical delivery and sustainable financing, Sri Lanka can turn its transport plans into lasting economic gains—improving mobility, strengthening business productivity and building a more connected and competitive nation

Efficient transport is fundamental to Sri Lanka’s economic growth. Shorter commuting times, reliable public transport and better connections between residential areas, commercial centres and regional economies can improve productivity and create lasting economic value.

The Government’s on-going commitment to infrastructure development, including the planned modernisation of Colombo’s suburban railway network, provides a strong foundation for further progress. Building on this direction, three planned transport initiatives deserve focused attention: the New Kelani Bridge–Athurugiriya elevated highway, the Colombo Light Rail Transit (LRT) project and railway modernisation.

1. Elevated Highway: New Kelani Bridge to Athurugiriya

The proposed 16.4 km elevated highway would connect New Kelani Bridge, through Orugodawatta, Dematagoda, Rajagiriya, Koswatta and Hokandara, to the Outer Circular Expressway at Athurugiriya. Its interchanges would improve access to Battaramulla, Malabe and important administrative and educational centres. The project was planned as a four-lane, access-controlled highway under a public-private partnership model.

An earlier parliamentary estimate put the project cost at Rs. 171.7 billion, with an 18-year Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Maintain-and-Transfer (DBFOMT) concession, including three years for construction. This is a historical estimate and must be updated before a new financing commitment is made.

The priority should be to update the feasibility study, refresh construction costs and traffic forecasts, and invite competitive proposals from qualified investors. The original phased alignment—from New Kelani Bridge to Rajagiriya and onwards to Athurugiriya—could provide a basis for sequencing construction, subject to updated engineering and economic assessments.

Financing proposals should compare toll-based concessions with availability-payment models, examining the implications for government expenditure, traffic risk and investor returns. Contracts should establish clear construction deadlines, maintenance standards and handback requirements, while environmental approvals and fair treatment of affected communities remain integral to implementation.

The objective is to connect Colombo’s eastern suburbs with the expressway network, improve access to employment centres and reduce congestion on heavily used roads.

2. Colombo LRT: Develop a sustainable financing model

The proposed 15.7 km Colombo LRT line from Fort to Malabe, via Battaramulla, was designed with 16 stations and an estimated journey time of approximately 30 minutes. In 2019, Japan offered a concessional yen-loan package of up to ¥30.04 billion, at 0.1% annual interest, with a 40-year repayment period and a 12-year grace period. These were the original terms, not a confirmed current financing offer. 

The Government has continued engagement with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA). In February 2026, Foreign Affairs Minister Vijitha Herath confirmed that discussions were ongoing, with no final agreement yet reached.

The next step should be a fresh technical and financial appraisal, examining updated construction costs, passenger demand, land requirements and long-term operating expenditure. Discussions with JICA should explore renewed concessional financing, revised project scope and the possibility of phased implementation.

Station-area commercial development, retail concessions and advertising could supplement fare revenue. However, the financial plan must also provide for routine maintenance, staffing, electricity and rolling-stock replacement, with any necessary operating subsidy transparently budgeted.

The long-term objective should remain a reliable, high-capacity urban transport system supported by a financially sustainable operating model.

3. Railway Development: Build on existing investment

Railway modernisation offers Sri Lanka an opportunity to build on its existing infrastructure and ongoing development partnerships.

In April 2026, the President’s Office announced plans for the first phase of electric train services on three Colombo suburban corridors: Maradana–Makumbura on the Kelani Valley Line, Fort–Ragama on the Main Line, and Fort–Panadura on the Coastal Line, with commencement planned for early 2027.

The active Asian Development Bank Railway Efficiency Improvement Project includes a $160 million loan within a total project cost of $192 million. Its objectives include improving railway operations, safety, maintenance facilities, ticketing systems and technical capacity.

Priority should be given to completing funded works, upgrading track and signalling infrastructure, improving train frequency and reliability, and ensuring that the new electric services are supported by adequate power supply, maintenance facilities and rolling stock.

Further investment should be guided by passenger demand and economic returns, including improved capacity on the Kelani Valley and other high-demand commuter routes. Integrated ticketing and convenient connections with buses would make rail a more practical option for daily commuters.

Operational funding is just as important as construction finance. Annual maintenance budgets, performance targets for punctuality and cancellations, and transparent reporting on passenger numbers and operating costs would help protect the value of public investment.

Lessons from Bangladesh and the Philippines

Regional experience demonstrates the importance of pairing infrastructure investment with sustainable financing and reliable operations.

Bangladesh’s Dhaka MRT Line 6 began commercial operations in December 2022, with services extended in November 2023. Its operator reported an average of 318,162 passengers daily between January and March 2026. This illustrates the potential scale of demand that a functioning urban mass-transit system can serve.

The Philippines provides a useful example of sustained railway rehabilitation. In March 2026, Japan’s JICA signed a further ¥21.6 billion loan for rehabilitation and maintenance of Metro Rail Transit Line 3. The 40-year loan carries a 10-year grace period and will fund upgrades to tracks, power systems, trains and maintenance equipment. Earlier rehabilitation restored operations to the line’s design speed of 60 km/h and reduced service interruptions. 

The lesson for Sri Lanka is to secure financing that matches each project’s needs, deliver improvements in manageable phases, and establish reliable maintenance and operating arrangements from the outset.

Prioritising investment for maximum impact

While the LRT remains an important long-term ambition, its substantial capital requirements and recurring operating costs may be difficult to accommodate immediately, even with concessional financing. In the near term, priority should therefore be given to advancing the New Kelani Bridge–Athurugiriya elevated highway and railway modernisation. A carefully structured public-private partnership could support the highway, while the railway programme can build on existing development-partner financing and planned electrification. The LRT should remain in the development pipeline, progressing towards implementation when updated feasibility studies, sustainable financing and a credible operating plan establish its affordability.

The Government’s wider development agenda provides an opportunity to bring these planned initiatives together under a clear transport investment roadmap, with defined milestones, transparent procurement, environmental safeguards and long-term maintenance arrangements.

By prioritising practical delivery and sustainable financing, Sri Lanka can turn its transport plans into lasting economic gains—improving mobility, strengthening business productivity and building a more connected and competitive nation.

(The author is the President, Ceylon Institute of Builders)
